description: Outdoor surface materials for the frequency-domain admittance method. CANONICAL SOURCE: the SurfaceTemps repository. The Eddy3D C# port embeds a byte-identical copy at Radiance.Core/Resources/outdoor_materials.json; if you edit this file you must copy it there, and both test suites pin the same values so drift is caught.
scoping_note: Each entry describes the EXPOSED OUTER LAYER, because that is what sets the surface temperature the downstream MRT calculation consumes. The layers behind it are given as a substrate stack, which matters only through the thermal mass it lends the outer layer. For a thermally thin outer layer (any metal skin) the substrate dominates entirely and is mandatory - see validation.structural.

absorptivity.note: Solar absorptivity alpha = 1 - solar reflectance (albedo). Below 0.15 is only fresh cool-white coatings and bare polished metal; above 0.95 only fresh black membranes and new asphalt.

emissivity.note: Long-wave emissivity is BIMODAL: bare or polished metals sit at 0.02-0.30, anodised or painted metals at 0.77-0.90, and all non-metals at 0.84-0.97. A value between 0.30 and 0.75 is only physical for partially oxidised metal and should warn. Emissivity is load-bearing: h_r = 4*eps*sigma*T^3, so mistaking a bare metal for masonry overstates its radiative coupling roughly twentyfold.

structural.note: Paper Eq. 5: tau = L*sqrt(pi*rho*c/(P*lambda)) for the diurnal period. An outer layer with tau < 0.01 stores no heat over a day (0.7 mm zinc gives tau ~ 2e-3), so without a substrate the solve degenerates to the internal boundary condition and returns a near-constant, meaningless temperature. Such entries MUST carry a substrate.

sand_bedding.source: CIBSE Guide A, damp bedding sand

materials.name: Asphalt, new
materials.source: alpha: ACPA albedo data (new asphalt albedo 0.05-0.10); eps: Oke, Boundary Layer Climates 2e Table 1.1; lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456:2007 Table 3
materials.notes: The hottest common urban surface. Ages lighter - see asphalt_weathered.

materials.name: Asphalt, weathered
materials.source: alpha: ACPA aged albedo 0.10-0.15; otherwise as asphalt_new
materials.notes: Reflective seal coats reach albedo 0.25-0.35 (alpha 0.65-0.75) - LBNL Heat Island Group.

materials.name: Concrete paving, grey
materials.source: alpha: GCCA/ACPA (new albedo 0.20-0.30, weathered ~0.25); eps: Oke Table 1.1; lambda/rho/c: CIBSE Guide A cast concrete
materials.notes: White or SCM concrete reaches albedo 0.5-0.7 (alpha 0.3-0.5).

materials.name: Granite sett, light grey
materials.source: alpha ESTIMATED from stone albedo 0.20-0.35; lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456 crystalline rock
materials.notes: High conductivity and mass: slow to heat, slow to cool.

materials.name: Clay brick paver, red
materials.source: alpha: ASHRAE Handbook of Fundamentals, red brick 0.63-0.77; eps: fired clay 0.86-0.93; lambda/rho/c: CIBSE Guide A brick

materials.name: Gravel, loose
materials.source: Bulk conductivity halved against ISO 10456 moist sand and gravel (2.0) to account for air voids; albedo 0.20-0.35 for grey aggregate

materials.name: Decomposed granite
materials.source: Dry sandy-soil analogue

materials.name: Artificial turf (3G)
materials.source: alpha/eps MEASURED (albedo 0.09, eps 0.95): Building & Environment 2025, doi:10.1016/j.buildenv.2025.112706; pile and infill thermal properties estimated
materials.notes: Reaches 90-95 C in field measurements - the hottest surface in this library, and unlike grass it has no evapotranspiration to lose.

materials.name: Natural grass, irrigated
materials.source: alpha: Oke grass albedo 0.16-0.26; eps: Oke 0.90-0.95; sod properties estimated for moist organic layer
materials.notes: WARNING: this model has no evapotranspiration, so daytime grass temperature is overestimated. Field measurement puts natural turf near 30 C where artificial turf hits 50 C under the same weather; the model cannot reproduce that gap.

materials.name: Bare soil, dry
materials.source: alpha: Oke soil albedo 0.05 (dark wet) to 0.40 (light dry); eps: Oke 0.90-0.98; lambda/rho/c: CIBSE Guide A topsoil
materials.notes: Moisture content swings conductivity by a factor of 2-3.

materials.name: Sand, dry
materials.source: alpha: Oke desert sand albedo 0.20-0.45; eps: Oke 0.84-0.91
materials.notes: Note the distinction from the sand_bedding substrate (1.74 W/mK), which is CIBSE's DAMP bedding sand under pavers. Using that value for a dry sand surface is roughly fivefold too conductive and halves the predicted peak excursion.

materials.name: Water, shallow
materials.source: alpha: Oke water albedo 0.03-0.10 at high sun; eps 0.92-0.97; lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456 water
materials.notes: OUT OF MODEL SCOPE: evaporation and convective mixing dominate a real water body, so a conduction-only admittance solve overshoots peak temperature badly. Provided for completeness; treat results as indicative only.

materials.name: Concrete, fair-faced
materials.source: alpha: ASHRAE HoF concrete absorptance 0.60-0.83; lambda/rho/c: CIBSE Guide A cast concrete

materials.name: Brick, red facade
materials.source: alpha: ASHRAE HoF red brick 0.63; lambda/rho/c: CIBSE Guide A brick
materials.notes: Matches the repository's original brick_wall build-up.

materials.name: Render, light cream
materials.source: alpha: ASHRAE HoF cream paint ~0.35, aged render 0.4-0.5; lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456 exterior render
materials.notes: Fresh white paint reaches alpha 0.23-0.26.

materials.name: Limestone, Portland
materials.source: albedo 0.35-0.55; lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456 sedimentary rock
materials.notes: Porous limestones run nearer ISO's light sedimentary row (lambda ~1.1).

materials.name: Sandstone, buff
materials.source: albedo 0.20-0.35; lambda/rho/c interpolated from ISO 10456 sedimentary rock rows

materials.name: Granite cladding, grey
materials.source: lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456 crystalline rock; polished stone eps 0.85-0.90
materials.notes: As a ventilated rainscreen the panel is largely decoupled from the wall behind it; the air gap in the substrate stack represents that. Dark granite reaches alpha ~0.88.

materials.name: Timber, weathered grey
materials.source: eps: wood 0.90; lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456 timber 500 kg/m3
materials.notes: New pale softwood is nearer alpha 0.45; a dark stain reaches 0.85.

materials.name: Weathering steel (Corten), rusted
materials.source: alpha: 'Solar properties of some building elements', Energy 1989, doi:10.1016/0360-5442(89)90034-0 (oxidised steels alpha_s 0.85-0.93); eps: rusted steel 0.80-0.90; lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456 steel
materials.notes: Thermally thin (diurnal tau ~ 1e-3): the panel itself stores nothing and its temperature is set by what sits behind it, so the substrate is mandatory.

materials.name: Aluminium, clear anodised
materials.source: alpha 0.36 / eps 0.80 measured for clear anodic film (thermal-control coating literature); lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456 aluminium alloys
materials.notes: Do NOT interpolate towards mill-finish aluminium: bare polished aluminium is alpha 0.10-0.15 with eps 0.03-0.09, so anodising raises emissivity roughly tenfold. They are different materials thermally.

materials.name: Glass curtain wall (DGU)
materials.source: eps: uncoated glass 0.84 (ASHRAE HoF, Fenestration); lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456 glass
materials.notes: OPAQUE APPROXIMATION: alpha here is only the fraction absorbed IN the outer pane. Between 0.4 and 0.6 of incident solar is TRANSMITTED through the assembly and never heats this surface node, so this entry models the pane's own temperature, not the glazing's energy balance.

materials.name: Zinc, pre-weathered standing seam
materials.source: eps: weathered zinc / galvanised patina 0.25-0.28 (polished zinc 0.05); lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456 zinc; alpha estimated from grey-patina reflectance 0.4-0.5
materials.notes: The low-emissivity case this library exists to express. With eps 0.25 the linearised h_r is about 1.4 W/m2K against 5.0 for masonry, so it sheds far less heat by radiation and runs much hotter than its moderate absorptivity suggests.

materials.name: Bitumen membrane, black
materials.source: LBNL Heat Island Group: black roof reflectance 0.05, emittance 0.90; lambda/rho/c: ISO 10456 bitumen
materials.notes: Matches the repository's original concrete_roof build-up.

materials.name: TPO membrane, white (cool roof)
materials.source: LBNL / CRRC: white membrane reflectance 0.80 initial, 0.65-0.70 aged; emittance 0.87-0.90
materials.notes: The cool-roof flagship, and the single largest lever this library expresses: alpha differs by about 0.7 from bitumen_membrane_black, worth roughly 30 K of peak surface temperature. Aged value is alpha ~0.32.

materials.name: Clay tile, terracotta
materials.source: LBNL red clay tile reflectance ~0.33; EN 1745 / CIBSE Guide A fired clay
materials.notes: Cool-colour tiles reach reflectance 0.40-0.60 at the same visual hue.

materials.name: Green roof, extensive
materials.source: albedo 0.20-0.25 and substrate properties: Sailor 2008, Energy & Buildings 40(8) / EnergyPlus EcoRoof defaults; eps 0.95 for vegetation
materials.notes: Same caveat as natural_grass: without evapotranspiration the model overestimates daytime temperature. Wet substrate conductivity rises towards 0.6.

materials.name: Metal roof, painted mid-grey
materials.source: Painted-metal emissivity 0.83-0.88 (the PAINT governs, not the steel); LBNL cool-colour metal reflectance 0.30-0.60
materials.notes: Conventional dark metal roofs reach alpha ~0.90; cool pigments cut alpha by 0.20-0.25 at the same hue. Contrast with zinc_preweathered, where the bare patina leaves emissivity low.

materials.name: Gravel ballast roof
materials.source: LBNL gravel-surfaced roof reflectance 0.12-0.34
